meta.purpose: Every value that could not be confirmed against an official source, every inconsistency found in the supplied data, and every modelling assumption that materially moves the answer. Nothing here blocks the analysis; everything here changes how much confidence the analysis deserves.
meta.convention: F-numbers are stable and referenced from the other pages and from VERIFICATION.md.

items.title: Property B's implied property tax rate is 2.14%, but San Francisco publishes 1.1816%
items.detail: The supplied 2025 figures are $2,439 of tax on a $114,248 assessment, which implies 2.1350%. San Francisco's published secured rate for FY 2026-27 is 1.18162182%. The gap is about $1,070 a year and has persisted for a decade — the implied rate ranges from 1.68% in 2016 to 2.14% in 2025. A ten-year consistent gap is more likely to be real parcel-level charges (special assessments, bond levies, a district charge outside the secured rate) or a second parcel appearing on the same bill, than a transcription error.
items.impact: The model uses the implied 2.135% so the projection matches the bills actually paid. If the true rate is 1.1816%, Property B's tax is overstated by roughly half, which raises every scenario's terminal value by a similar amount because Property B is held in all three — so the ranking does not change, but every absolute number does.
items.action: Obtain one actual Property B tax bill and read the rate line and the special-assessment lines.

items.title: Property A's implied rate is 1.3352%, against a county illustration of 1.1488%
items.detail: $7,207 of tax on a $539,743 assessment implies 1.3352%. Santa Clara County's own booklet illustrates a typical tax rate area at 1.1488% per $100. A 16% excess — roughly $1,000 a year — is easily explained by a tax rate area carrying more bond load, but it cannot be confirmed without the parcel number, which is deliberately not recorded.
items.impact: The model uses 1.3352%. The county's 1.1488% is run as a sensitivity on the Decision analysis page.
items.action: Read the rate line on an actual Property A bill.

items.title: Property A 2017: tax fell 0.5% while the assessment rose 2%
items.detail: The supplied row shows $6,383 of tax in both 2017 and 2018, with the assessment rising 2% each year. A constant-rate model cannot produce a falling tax against a rising assessment.
items.impact: Kept exactly as supplied. Does not affect the projections, which start from the 2026 row.
items.action: If the 2017 figure is a typo, correct it in the source records for cleanliness.

items.title: Property A 2020: tax identical to 2019 while the assessment rose 2%
items.detail: Both years show $6,565 of tax, with the assessment rising from $483,854 to $493,530.
items.impact: Kept as supplied. No effect on the projections.
items.action: Same as F3.

items.title: Property A's 2026 property tax is blank
items.detail: The request shows `--` for 2026. No 2026-27 bill exists at the research date, so no value is inferred. The assessment figure for 2026 is present and is used.
items.impact: The model starts from the 2025 tax figure projected forward at the 2% assessment cap, and uses the supplied 2026 assessment as the baseline for assessed value.
items.action: Fill in when the 2026-27 bill arrives.

items.title: Which property is the parents' principal residence is not stated
items.detail: Proposition 19's parent-child exclusion applies only to a family home that is the transferor's principal residence and becomes the transferee's principal residence. If Property A is not the parents' principal residence for tax purposes — and it matters whether they have claimed a homeowners' exemption there — the exclusion is unavailable entirely.
items.impact: The live-in scenario is modelled assuming Property A qualifies. If it does not, the live-in scenario collapses to the rent-out scenario's tax treatment and the analysis changes materially.
items.action: Confirm the homeowners' exemption on Property A's bill and confirm the parents' principal residence for tax purposes.

items.title: Insurance premiums are user estimates, not official figures
items.detail: Both properties are modelled at $1,500 a year. No official body publishes a parcel-level or ZIP-level homeowner premium — not the California Department of Insurance, not the NAIC. Several commercial comparison sites were found offering county-level 'averages' that disagreed with each other by a factor of three; none is used or cited.
items.impact: Insurance is the weakest input in the model. It is escalated at general inflation, which is probably too slow given recent California rate increases. Doubling Property A's premium to $3,000 changes its terminal value by a measurable but not decision-changing amount (shown on the Decision analysis page).
items.action: Get real quotes for both properties, including landlord coverage for Property B.

items.title: The solar interconnection date is unknown, so the applicable export tariff is unknown
items.detail: The CPUC closed the net-energy-metering tariffs to new enrollments; interconnections applied for on or after April 15, 2023 take the Net Billing Tariff, which pays avoided-cost value for exports rather than retail rates. The solar on Property A currently produces a net credit, which suggests a retail-rate tariff — but the interconnection date was not supplied.
items.impact: Modelled as a $15/month credit with a $0 floor sensitivity. If the system is later re-tariffed, the credit could shrink to near zero. This is small money relative to the decision but it is real.
items.action: Find the interconnection agreement or the original solar contract date.

items.title: Property A market value and Property B market value are user estimates
items.detail: $3,100,000 and $1,800,000 as of November 2026. No appraisal or automated valuation from an official source was used, and none could be obtained without the address.
items.impact: Every projection scales with these. A 10% error on Property A moves the live-in terminal value by roughly the same proportion.
items.action: Obtain an appraisal or a broker opinion of value for each property.

items.title: The cash amount in the inheritance is deliberately not recorded
items.detail: Privacy policy: the amount is never written down anywhere in this project. Instead, all estate-tax headroom figures are expressed as 'the amount of other assets that could be added before the exclusion is reached', so the answer to 'how much is too much' is available without the real number appearing.
items.impact: None on the analysis. It does mean the estate-tax page cannot state a single headline exposure figure.
items.action: Read the headroom column on the Estate & inheritance tax page.

items.title: The federal estate-tax exclusion after 2026 has not been published
items.detail: The exclusion is $15,000,000 for 2026 and is indexed for inflation from 2027 under the enacted legislation, but the IRS has not published the forward amounts.
items.impact: Every year after 2026 in the estate table uses the 2026 figure as a FLOOR. The real exclusion will be higher, so the modelled estate-tax exposure is an upper bound. This is conservative in the right direction for planning.
items.action: Update annually from the IRS's inflation-adjustment release.

items.title: The California rate applied to capital gains is a 9.3% planning blend
items.detail: California taxes capital gains as ordinary income with no preferential rate. The actual marginal rate depends on total taxable income in the year of sale, ranging from 1% to 13.3%. 9.3% is a mid-bracket planning assumption, not a verified rate for any specific year.
items.impact: A 13.3% marginal rate would raise the liquidation tax on the held scenarios noticeably; a lower rate would reduce it. It does not change the ranking.
items.action: Model the actual sale year's income with a CPA.

items.title: Land share of Property A's value is assumed at 60%
items.detail: Land is not depreciable, so the land/improvement split determines how much depreciation shelter a rented-out Property A generates. The split cannot be obtained without the assessor's parcel record.
items.impact: Only affects the rent-out scenario's income tax. A 50%–70% range is plausible.
items.action: Look up the land/improvement split on the assessor's record.

items.title: Property A's actual tax rate area cannot be determined
items.detail: Composite property tax rates in Santa Clara County vary by tax rate area, which can only be looked up with the assessor's parcel number. Privacy policy forbids recording the parcel number.
items.impact: The model uses the rate implied by the property's own bills, which is a reasonable proxy, and shows the county's illustrative rate beside it.
items.action: Read the rate line on the bill; no parcel number needed for that.

items.title: The Prop 19 value allowance for a 2040–2050 transfer has not been published
items.detail: The allowance is $1,044,586 for transfers from 2/16/2025 through 2/15/2027. It is adjusted every other February to the FHFA California House Price Index. The forward amounts do not exist yet.
items.impact: The model holds $1,044,586 flat. Because the FHFA California index has been rising, the real allowance is likely to be much larger by 2040 — which means the model is CONSERVATIVE FOR THE HEIR on this point and the live-in scenario is understated.
items.action: Update when each biennial adjustment is published.

items.title: Property B has three units, so the AB 1482 owner-occupied duplex exemption does not fit
items.detail: Civil Code §1947.12(d)(6) exempts a single structure containing two dwelling units where the owner occupies one. Property B contains three. So even living on site does not exempt Property B from the statewide cap on that basis.
items.impact: Affects how much rent Property B can raise. Not modelled as a legal entitlement — the model uses a flat 2%/yr assumption regardless.
items.action: Confirm the building's certificate-of-occupancy date to determine whether the SF Rent Ordinance (pre-June 13, 1979) or only AB 1482 applies.

items.title: Rent growth of 2% a year is an assumption, and AB 1482 sunsets in 2030
items.detail: The model applies 2%/yr rent growth across a multi-decade horizon. Legally, nothing entitles a landlord to that: San Francisco's allowable increase is 1.6% for 2026–27, and the statewide AB 1482 cap is repealed as of January 1, 2030 as written. Whether it is extended is unknown.
items.impact: Rent growth is the second-largest driver of the rent-out scenario. The model deliberately assumes neither an extension nor a lapse.
items.action: Re-check the statute each year; treat any projection past 2030 as conditional.

items.title: The rent for Property A if rented out is an assumption with no official source
items.detail: No official rent exists for this specific home. A HUD Fair Market Rent cross-check was attempted, but the HUD FMR query table did not return values in this research pass, so no HUD figure is claimed or shown. $5,400/month is a planning assumption.
items.impact: This is the input the rent-out scenario is most sensitive to. The $4,500–$7,000 range is modelled explicitly and shown on the Decision analysis page.
items.action: Obtain a rental appraisal or comparable listings for the address.

items.title: Utility rates beyond FY 2027-28 have not been published
items.detail: SFPUC adopted a two-year rate schedule (FY 2026-27 and FY 2027-28) and San Jose Water's Schedule 1 is effective July 1, 2026 with a general rate case in progress. Nothing official exists through 2065.
items.impact: Utilities are escalated at 2.5%/yr general inflation. SFPUC's own published second-year increase is about 7% on the service charge, which is faster than that — so the model probably understates future utility cost.
items.action: Re-index when new schedules are adopted.

items.title: Earthquake insurance is not modelled at all
items.detail: Standard California homeowners policies exclude earthquake. No coverage amount or premium was supplied, and none can be verified at parcel level.
items.impact: Carried at zero, so every projection is slightly optimistic. For two pre-1980 Bay Area structures this is a real exposure, not a rounding error.
items.action: Get a California Earthquake Authority quote for each property.

items.title: Cost of sale is assumed at 6% of gross price
items.detail: Assumes roughly a 5% brokerage commission plus escrow, title and recording, with the county documentary transfer tax applied separately from its published rate. Commissions are negotiable and not published.
items.impact: A 5%–7% range is plausible. Small relative to the decision margin.
items.action: Replace with actual quotes when a sale is real.

items.title: Home price appreciation of 3% a year is an assumption, and it drives both scenarios
items.detail: Anchored to the FHFA all-transactions California index, which compounded at about 3.8% from 2004Q1 to 2026Q2. The base case sits below that because the index grew only 0.90% in the last year and Cupertino's population fell 3.2% between 2020 and 2025.
items.impact: This is the largest single driver of both the live-in and rent-out terminal values. The 2%–4% range is shown explicitly. Note the asymmetry: higher appreciation helps the hold scenarios but also raises the liquidation tax on them.
items.action: Nothing to fix — but re-read the sensitivity table before relying on any single figure.

items.title: The reinvestment return of 6.5% is the single assumption the recommendation is most sensitive to
items.detail: 6.5% nominal before tax for a balanced portfolio, cross-checked against a Treasury curve that put the 10-year at 4.38%, the 20-year at 5.29% and the 30-year at 5.26% on 2026-11-09. Nothing guarantees 6.5%.
items.impact: At 4.5% the sell-and-reinvest case loses most or all of its advantage; at 8.5% the advantage widens substantially. The break-even is computed and shown rather than left implicit.
items.action: Decide what return is actually achievable for this heir's risk tolerance, then re-read the break-even.

items.title: Probate savings from the trust are not quantified
items.detail: A funded revocable trust is the standard California tool for avoiding probate on real property. Whether the trust is actually funded is unknown, and California statutory probate fees depend on the estate's facts.
items.impact: Not modelled at all. If the trust is NOT funded, both properties go through probate and the process timeline and cost change substantially — but no direction on the decision itself.
items.action: Confirm that both properties are titled in the trust's name.

items.title: Property B's basis at liquidation is proxied by its assessed value
items.detail: The terminal-value calculation for Property B uses the existing assessed value as a stand-in for the owners' actual cost basis, which is unknown.
items.impact: Affects the capital-gains tax on a hypothetical Property B sale at the horizon. Because Property B is held in all three scenarios, this shifts every scenario's terminal value by the same amount and does not change the ranking.
items.action: Confirm the actual purchase price and any capitalised improvements.
